origin.title: Delay-Tolerant Networking Architecture
origin.summary: The DTN architecture treats interruptions as a normal property of a network. A device retains a complete message and forwards it when a suitable contact appears, instead of requiring a continuous path between sender and recipient. RFC 4838 documents this store-and-forward architecture; Bundle Protocol version 7 later standardized its message format.

history.summary: DTN is implemented and standardized. The opportunity is an understandable, community-operated notice service built on that foundation.
history.whatWasBuilt: The Bundle Protocol has multiple implementations. dtn7-rs provides a BP7 daemon, routing strategies, command-line tools, network discovery, and application interfaces. The transport can therefore be reused for the notice service.
history.whatRemains: This proposal adds a complete experience for composing, relaying, expiring, acknowledging, and correcting ordinary notices. A sender needs to distinguish stored locally, copied to a relay, received by a destination, and actually acknowledged; those states should remain intelligible after several disconnected hops.

whyNow.summary: A library, traveling workshop, or rural association could test whether scheduled encounters make useful communications possible with fewer assumptions about connectivity. The proposed benefit is continuity for low-urgency coordination. It must be demonstrated through delivery trials rather than inferred from a successful network demo.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Deliver 100 numbered test notices between three isolated local networks through one periodically connected relay, then reconcile receipts.

steps.title: Make the interruption visible
steps.description: Build a local outbox and inbox above dtn7-rs. Give every notice an identifier, destination, expiry, size limit, and status explanation that remains readable without a connection.
steps.deliverable: A working notice composer with a durable queue.

steps.title: Exercise scheduled encounters
steps.description: Connect relay nodes on a fixed schedule, deliberately interrupt transfers, and record which notices arrived, expired, or were duplicated. Compare routing settings with the same replayable contact pattern.
steps.deliverable: A reproducible three-network delivery experiment.

steps.title: Test the human handoff
steps.description: Ask volunteers to operate relays without a developer. Add clear storage limits, contact summaries, and a recovery procedure for a lost or full device.
steps.deliverable: An operator guide and usability report with delivery measurements.

successCriteria: Every received notice maps to a single original despite duplicate transport.
Expired notices are marked clearly and never presented as current.
Volunteers can explain the difference between relayed and acknowledged without assistance.
nonGoals: New radio hardware or replacement of the Bundle Protocol

roles.contribution: Build the contact schedule and instrument transport behavior.

roles.name: Application developer
roles.contribution: Implement message state, receipts, and recovery.

roles.name: Community organizer
roles.contribution: Choose realistic notices and evaluate volunteer operation.

challenges.title: Delivery is not guaranteed
challenges.description: BP7 does not itself promise end-to-end arrival. Application receipts, expiry, and an explicit unknown state are essential; a green icon must not imply that a person has read a notice.

challenges.title: Relay trust and storage
challenges.description: A relay can withhold messages or run out of space. Begin with synthetic, non-sensitive notices and known operators; define authentication, retention, and abuse limits before handling real community information.

origin.title: E and capability-based distributed cooperation
origin.summary: The original E documentation describes distributed programs that cooperate through references carrying specific authority. An object can reach another object only after receiving an appropriate reference. This offers a way to express a limited relationship, such as access to one document, instead of trusting an application with everything a user owns.

history.summary: Capability systems exist. The unfinished product direction here is making delegated authority legible and manageable for a small community organization.
history.whatWasBuilt: E implemented a capability-oriented programming model. Cap’n Proto later built an RPC system informed by E’s CapTP protocol, including remote object references and promise pipelining. Its MIT-licensed implementation is the reusable foundation selected here.
history.whatRemains: Build a concrete permission experience around those primitives: a reminder tool may read the date of one booking but cannot browse the membership directory; a volunteer can hand off a temporary role; an owner can revoke a delegation and see its consequences. The experiment would test these application behaviors with a small volunteer organization.

whyNow.summary: Volunteer organizations often combine tools maintained by different people. A small equipment library provides a manageable setting to test whether permission by task is easier to understand than accumulating broad integrations. The expected benefit is reduced accidental exposure and easier handover when a volunteer leaves; both require testing with actual workflows.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Connect three local services for a fictional tool library and demonstrate that a booking-only integration cannot enumerate members or change inventory.

steps.title: Define authority as an interface
steps.description: Model inventory lookup, booking creation, and reminder delivery as separate interfaces. Start with synthetic members and explicit trust boundaries between processes.
steps.deliverable: A runnable service example and documented permission graph.

steps.title: Make delegation understandable
steps.description: Build a screen that explains the object, allowed actions, holder, expiry policy, and parent delegation. Implement revocation using an application-level intermediary and exercise a handover.
steps.deliverable: A usable permission inspector with a tested revocation path.

steps.title: Try realistic mistakes
steps.description: Have volunteers connect the wrong tool, share a capability too widely, and retire an account. Record whether the interface makes the problem detectable and recoverable.
steps.deliverable: An adversarial test set and a volunteer usability report.

successCriteria: The reminder service cannot access fields beyond its declared interface.
Revocation blocks new calls through the revoked intermediary.
Participants correctly predict the scope of a delegation before sharing it.
nonGoals: A promise to retract information already copied by an authorized recipient

challenges.title: Revocation has a boundary
challenges.description: Stopping future calls cannot erase data already received. The interface must distinguish ongoing authority from information that has already left the service.

challenges.title: Ambient authority can return
challenges.description: A narrow RPC interface does not help if its implementation also has unnecessary filesystem, database, or network access. Trace authority through the whole service, including fallback and recovery paths.

origin.title: Federated Wiki and Folk Memory
origin.summary: Federated Wiki began as a small implementation of a broader Folk Memory vision. Instead of editing only one shared page on one server, participants own sites and copy pages into new contexts. The project’s own history describes its 2011 beginning and the later separation of client, server, and plugins.

history.summary: Federated Wiki already supports this publishing model. The proposed experiment makes local adaptation useful for a real network of repair groups.
history.whatWasBuilt: Federated Wiki has working servers, a browser client, plugins, and a federation of sites. The Node.js package assembles these components and documents running a personal server and seeding a neighborhood of related sites.
history.whatRemains: Create a handbook workflow that records which equipment and circumstances a procedure applies to, why a group changed it, who tested the change, and where an earlier version can be found. Build comparison and update notices around that context rather than treating every different page as an error to be merged.

whyNow.summary: Repair collectives can benefit from one another’s discoveries while serving different communities and equipment. This proposal tests whether federation helps knowledge travel without erasing useful disagreement. The benefit would be a maintained network of practical learning, measured by successful reuse and clear attribution rather than the number of copied pages.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Run three independently owned wikis and follow ten software troubleshooting guides as each group adapts and tests them.

steps.title: Establish a small commons
steps.description: Agree on a content license and a guide template containing prerequisites, software version, evidence, and local contact. Seed ten original software repair guides on separate sites.
steps.deliverable: Three running sites and ten deliberately licensed guides.

steps.title: Show the path of an adaptation
steps.description: Add a comparison view that traces page origins, identifies changed steps, and records the reason for a local variation. Let authors subscribe to relevant upstream changes without automatic replacement.
steps.deliverable: A provenance and comparison workflow tested across sites.

steps.title: Test knowledge handover
steps.description: Give a new volunteer a guide from another group. Observe whether they can identify the applicable version, contact its maintainer, and publish a verified correction.
steps.deliverable: A study of ten cross-group uses and a maintenance agreement.

successCriteria: Every adapted guide retains an identifiable source and content license.
Readers can distinguish tested steps from untested suggestions.
Each group can export its own pages and continue independently.
nonGoals: A universal encyclopedia or mandatory consensus

roles.name: Web developer
roles.contribution: Implement comparison and update workflows with the existing wiki components.

roles.name: Technical writer
roles.contribution: Develop the guide format and version conventions.

roles.name: Repair volunteer
roles.contribution: Write, test, and adapt guides in real sessions.

challenges.title: Versions need context
challenges.description: Two pages can differ because both are correct for different software releases. Present prerequisites and evidence next to the differences so that a newer edit does not automatically look more authoritative.

challenges.title: A federation needs care
challenges.description: Independent ownership also means broken links, inactive maintainers, and differing moderation standards. Start with named stewards and test exports and replacements before adding more sites.

origin.title: A server people control, operated by someone they trust
origin.summary: Sandstorm’s stated mission was to make independent web applications practical for ordinary people. Its proposal allowed a friend, organization, or service to administer a server while users installed their own applications. Isolating those applications was part of making that delegated operation possible.

history.summary: Sandstorm exists as a usable platform. This brief revives the ownership ambition through a specific continuity and stewardship experiment.
history.whatWasBuilt: Sandstorm provides a self-hostable application platform, isolated application instances, installation tooling, and documentation for backups. Its project history records a transition from a funded team to community development in 2017.
history.whatRemains: Create a complete operating model for a small association: a plain-language service inventory, named backup stewards, maintenance windows, understandable recovery status, and a rehearsed transfer to a new administrator. The next step is organizational continuity around working software.

whyNow.summary: A community’s digital records should remain usable when the technically confident volunteer moves away. A cooperative hosting kit could reduce that single-person dependency while preserving local choice of tools. Hosting, labor, and storage still cost money; the experiment is about control and recoverability rather than promising free infrastructure.

steps.title: Define the operating agreement

Members can export their app data through a documented route.

origin.title: Secure Scuttlebutt’s locally held social histories
origin.summary: Secure Scuttlebutt organizes communication as signed histories held on participants’ devices. Peers exchange the parts of those histories they lack when connections become available. The ssb-db component records this model directly: an identity signs an ordered feed, allowing another peer to verify who wrote a message and where it belongs.

history.summary: Scuttlebutt has working social applications and protocol components. This proposal tests a narrow coordination problem where stale information must be handled explicitly.
history.whatWasBuilt: ssb-db stores and verifies signed append-only feeds and provides interfaces for reading and publishing messages. The protocol guide explains identity, replication, discovery, and private messages. The application can build on these existing components.
history.whatRemains: Make an offer-and-request workflow that remains understandable when two neighbors act before either sees the other’s update. Record offered, tentatively claimed, confirmed, completed, and expired states without pretending disconnected peers share an immediate global truth. Add consent and retention explanations before inviting a real group.

whyNow.summary: A group sharing garden tools or surplus materials could use a local board during an internet outage or at a gathering without reliable service. The test is whether delayed coordination helps with ordinary, non-sensitive tasks. It should not be presented as emergency communication or as a confidential case-management system.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Let five test participants post and tentatively claim fictional offers while disconnected, then reconcile the board after peers meet.

steps.title: Build the offer state machine
steps.description: Publish signed events for a small set of offer states. Show the last known update and keep a tentative claim distinct from the offer owner’s confirmation.
steps.deliverable: A local board backed by verifiable feed events.

steps.title: Make conflicts ordinary
steps.description: Simulate two people claiming one item before synchronization. Preserve both requests and ask the owner to resolve the conflict with a new signed event.
steps.deliverable: Repeatable conflict scenarios with clear explanations.

steps.title: Explain participation and exit
steps.description: Test onboarding, lost-device recovery, local blocking, and retirement of a profile with volunteers using synthetic data. Show that removing a local copy cannot erase peers’ copies.
steps.deliverable: A consent flow and a documented exit exercise.

successCriteria: No tentative claim silently becomes a confirmed commitment.
All peers eventually display the same owner-confirmed outcome after receiving the same events.
Participants can explain the retention and deletion limits before posting.
nonGoals: Emergency response or sensitive support records
Guaranteed global deletion of replicated messages

roles.contribution: Explain stale state, confirmation, and retention.

challenges.description: Append-only replication makes history useful but limits erasure. Local deletion does not recall a message already copied elsewhere; avoid personal or sensitive data in the initial experiment.

challenges.title: Identity and social trust differ
challenges.description: A valid signature identifies a key, not a trustworthy person. The group still needs an invitation process, a way to report abuse, and a recovery policy for lost keys.

origin.title: Babel’s routing design for changing networks
origin.summary: The experimental Babel specification described a routing protocol intended to remain useful as links change, including in wireless mesh networks. It combines distance-vector routing with rules that limit looping and allow recovery after a route disappears. Its design acknowledges tradeoffs such as update traffic and convergence time.

history.summary: Babel is a standardized protocol with existing implementations. The opportunity is participatory understanding and rehearsal for the people operating a local network.
history.whatWasBuilt: babeld implements the routing protocol. RFC 8966 later standardized an updated version, documenting behavior, security considerations, and limitations. The protocol already handles route selection; the rehearsal environment would expose and explain that behavior.
history.whatRemains: Create a software-only rehearsal environment that connects observable routing events to a map a volunteer can understand. A participant should be able to remove a link, see which destinations become unreachable, compare recovery paths, and export the exact experiment for another operator to replay.

whyNow.summary: Community connectivity is easier to maintain when more than one person understands what happens after a failure. A repeatable simulation could support training and shared planning without purchasing radio equipment or touching production routes. Its value is a better-informed operating team, to be measured through diagnosis tasks and recovery exercises.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Run six isolated babeld nodes in a virtual topology, remove two links, and render a replay explaining the resulting reachability changes.

steps.title: Build a repeatable virtual network
steps.description: Create isolated network namespaces or containers with explicit links, delay, and packet-loss parameters. Store topology and random seeds in a portable scenario file.
steps.deliverable: A six-node lab that produces the same events on replay.

steps.title: Connect routes to explanations
steps.description: Collect route changes and link observations without inspecting message payloads. Present destination reachability, next-hop changes, and confidence in observations alongside the map.
steps.deliverable: An interactive event timeline with readable route explanations.

steps.title: Run volunteer diagnosis sessions
steps.description: Ask operators to explain three injected failures before and after using the replay. Record mistaken assumptions and improve terminology and exercises.
steps.deliverable: A small training pack with measured diagnosis results.

successCriteria: A second operator can replay the same topology and failure sequence.
The view distinguishes measured state from a simulated prediction.
Participants can identify a broken path and describe at least one recovery option.
nonGoals: New radio hardware or antenna planning
Automatic changes to a live network

origin.title: IPFS: Content Addressed, Versioned, P2P File System
origin.summary: The IPFS paper proposed identifying files by their content and locating matching copies across peers. A stable content identifier allows a reader to verify the bytes obtained from a different host. The vision separates the identity of information from the continued availability of its original web server.

history.summary: IPFS is built and used. This proposal addresses a preservation workflow that content addressing alone does not supply.
history.whatWasBuilt: Kubo is an existing IPFS implementation with tools for adding, finding, retrieving, and pinning content. Official documentation explains that cached objects may be garbage-collected and that pinning expresses an intention to retain selected objects.
history.whatRemains: Turn storage primitives into an accountable agreement among archive stewards: who promises to keep which collection, how often recovery is checked, what happens when a volunteer leaves, and how collection descriptions and permissions are preserved with the bytes. A content hash proves identity, not permanent availability or historical truth.

whyNow.summary: A local history group or community software project could distribute custody of a modest, clearly licensed collection among several organizations. The potential benefit is resilience against a single neglected server. That benefit depends on funded storage, active stewards, and successful restore drills; a decentralized identifier by itself does not preserve anything.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Preserve 500 openly licensed test files across three steward nodes and recover the entire collection after taking the original publisher offline.

steps.title: Package a collection responsibly
steps.description: Create a manifest with file identifiers, titles, provenance, content licenses, and retention decisions. Begin with original or explicitly reusable public material.

steps.title: Make custody inspectable
steps.description: Let stewards accept named collections and report successful checks. Periodically fetch sampled blocks and schedule full restoration drills instead of trusting a node’s claim that it holds a copy.
steps.deliverable: A custody dashboard that distinguishes claims from verified retrievals.

steps.title: Rehearse loss and succession
steps.description: Disconnect the publisher, remove one steward, and restore onto a clean node from the others. Transfer the departing steward’s responsibilities and record failures.
steps.deliverable: A recovery report and a tested succession procedure.

origin.title: Dat’s distributed dataset synchronization vision
origin.summary: The Dat whitepaper described synchronizing large, changing folders while preserving verifiable dataset versions. Its protocol materials presented a public-key-addressed archive whose updates are signed and whose hosting can move without making identity depend on one server. The aim was reusable, distributed data rather than a single download location.

history.summary: Dat and later Hypercore software have implemented important parts of this direction. This experiment focuses on understandable publication and stewardship for a citizen-science group.
history.whatWasBuilt: Hypercore provides signed, verifiable data logs, selective replication, and APIs for data updates and snapshots. Its documentation explicitly notes incompatibility with older releases and supports truncation; it should not be described as an automatically immutable archive.
history.whatRemains: Add a publication workflow that binds an analysis to an explicit version, records corrections without confusing readers, separates observations from interpretations, and transfers mirroring responsibilities when a publisher leaves. Test those behaviors using synthetic temperature observations before collecting real personal or location-sensitive data.

whyNow.summary: Volunteer monitoring projects need others to inspect how a chart was produced and to retain useful data after a project changes hands. Versioned publication could make correction and independent reanalysis easier. The proposed benefit is reproducibility and continuity; signatures establish who controlled a publishing key, not whether a sensor reading is scientifically valid.

steps.title: Make correction traceable
steps.description: Build a release comparison showing added records, corrected values, and the stated reason for each change. Keep analyses attached to the release they actually used.
steps.deliverable: A version browser and chart-generation example.

steps.title: Exercise independent custody
steps.description: Replicate selected releases to a second node, disconnect the original publisher, and rerun the analyses. Document how the group replaces a lost signing key and preserves earlier citations.
steps.deliverable: A mirror recovery report and key-succession procedure.

successCriteria: A chart can be regenerated from its named release without the original publisher.

origin.title: YaCy’s search commons vision
origin.summary: YaCy’s philosophy argues that access to open information also depends on transparent search. Its author’s 2012 presentation described a complete search appliance combining crawling, indexing, administration, and a user interface, alongside a wider peer-to-peer search ambition. The historical vision includes communities choosing what they index and how results are ranked.

history.summary: YaCy is a working search engine. The proposed unfinished direction is a well-governed, usable search commons for a bounded public-interest collection.
history.whatWasBuilt: YaCy already includes a crawler, an index, a search interface, administration tools, and optional peer-to-peer index exchange. Its repository documents local-only searches and operation without participating in the public cluster.
history.whatRemains: Create a community editorial and operating layer: members propose sources, maintainers document acceptance or rejection, readers see why a result appears, and changes to ranking can be compared. Start with a small set of public technical learning resources and make the limits of the collection explicit.

whyNow.summary: A public library or community computing group could help readers discover useful resources without making each query depend on an external search account. A bounded corpus allows volunteers to evaluate coverage and errors. Privacy depends on deployment and logging choices, so this proposal specifically tests local-only processing rather than repeating claims of universal anonymity.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Index a consented set of 50 open learning sites and evaluate 40 realistic questions through a locally operated search portal.

steps.title: Define the collection and permissions
steps.description: Ask librarians and educators to nominate sources, record why each belongs, and check indexing permissions and content terms. Configure crawl limits and exclude private network discovery.
steps.deliverable: A public collection policy and a reviewed source list.

steps.title: Expose useful ranking evidence
steps.description: Present source, document date when known, matched terms, and collection context. Allow a reader to report stale or misleading results and publish a history of editorial changes.
steps.deliverable: A search interface with source explanations and correction requests.

steps.title: Evaluate quality and query handling
steps.description: Run the agreed questions, compare ranking adjustments, and inspect network requests and logs. Keep results processing local and measure gaps with librarians rather than claiming general-web coverage.
steps.deliverable: A relevance report and a documented query-data lifecycle.

successCriteria: Readers can see the search collection’s boundaries and propose corrections.
At least two maintainers can reproduce indexing and ranking changes.
The pilot sends no search queries to external engines or the public peer network.
nonGoals: Copying or redistributing source documents merely because they are publicly accessible

roles.name: Search developer
roles.contribution: Configure crawling and implement result explanations.

roles.name: Librarian or curator
roles.contribution: Define inclusion rules and judge retrieval quality.

roles.name: Operations engineer
roles.contribution: Verify local query handling, updates, and recovery.

challenges.title: Community selection still creates bias
challenges.description: An open index is not automatically representative. Publish selection criteria, rejected-source reasons, and evaluation failures; provide a route for the people served to challenge the collection.

challenges.title: Discovery does not transfer rights
challenges.description: Public access and permission to index are different from permission to republish complete documents. Keep attribution and content terms visible and design the pilot around sources that allow its intended use.

relatedWork.title: YaCy search server
relatedWork.relationship: The existing full search application; this proposal builds a local community collection and governance workflow around it.

references.title: YaCy — Philosophy
references.supports: The project’s historical argument for transparent, decentralized, user-governed search; its broad promises are treated as aspirations, not proven outcomes.
